title: Yayoi Kusama
wiki_lead:
Yayoi Kusama (草間 彌生, Kusama Yayoi; 22 March 1929 – 14 August 2026) was a Japanese artist who worked primarily in sculpture and installation. She was also active in painting, performance art, video art, fashion, poetry, and fiction. Rooted in conceptual art, her work incorporates elements of feminist art, minimalism, surrealism, art brut, pop art, and abstract expressionism, and is infused with autobiographical, psychological, and sexual themes. Acknowledged as one of the most important artists to emerge from Japan, she was among the world's top-selling female artists, ranking 19th on Sotheby's 2023 list of the top 50 artists. Her work influenced her contemporaries, including Andy Warhol and Claes Oldenburg.
Raised in Matsumoto, Kusama trained for a year at the Kyoto Municipal School of Arts and Crafts in the traditional Japanese painting style nihonga. Drawn to European and American avant-garde movements—particularly abstract expressionism—she moved to New York City in 1958 and was a part of the New York avant-garde scene throughout the 1960s, especially in the pop art movement. Embracing the rise of the hippie counterculture of the late 1960s, she came to public attention when she organized a series of happenings in which nude participants were painted with brightly colored polka dots. Although her work was largely overlooked during the 1970s, critical and popular interest revived in the late 1980s, leading to major retrospectives and permanent installations at museums worldwide.
Open about her struggles with mental illness, Kusama voluntarily resided in a Tokyo psychiatric hospital from 1977 until her death, crediting art as her primary means of coping with her condition. "I fight pain, anxiety, and fear every day, and the only method I have found that relieved my illness is to keep creating art", she told an interviewer in 2012. "I followed the thread of art and somehow discovered a path that would allow me to live."

"I fight pain, anxiety, and fear every day, and the only method I have found that relieved my illness is to keep creating art", she told an interviewer in 2012. "I followed the thread of art and somehow discovered a path that would allow me to live."


Life and career


Early life: 1929–1949
Yayoi Kusama was born on 22 March 1929 in Matsumoto, Nagano. Born into a merchant family that owned a plant nursery and seed farm, Kusama began drawing pumpkins in elementary school and depicting imagery from her visual hallucinations—motifs that would later define her career. Her mother was not supportive of her creative endeavors; Kusama would rush to finish her art because her mother would take it away to discourage her. Her mother was physically abusive, and she remembered her father as "the type who would play around, who would womanize a lot". She said her mother would often send her to spy on her father's extramarital affairs, which instilled in her a lifelong aversion to sexuality, particularly the male body and the phallus: "I don't like sex. I had an obsession with sex. When I was a child, my father had lovers and I experienced seeing him. My mother sent me to spy on him. I didn't want to have sex with anyone for years ... The sexual obsession and fear of sex sit side by side in me." Pumpkins, which became a central motif in her art, first captivated her during a childhood visit to a large seed-harvesting ground with her grandfather. She recalled being "enchanted by their charming and winsome form" and their "generous unpretentiousness", despite their humble status.
At age ten, Kusama began experiencing vivid hallucinations that she described as "flashes of light, auras, or dense fields of dots", including talking flowers and fabric patterns that appeared to come to life, multiply, and engulf her. Art became her refuge from both her family and her hallucinations, and she translated this sensation of being absorbed into her surroundings into an artistic practice she termed "self-obliteration". She also cited the smooth white stones covering the riverbed near her family home as a formative influence on her lifelong fixation with dots.
During the Pacific War, when Kusama was 13, she was sent to work in a military factory where she was tasked with making parachutes for the Imperial Japanese Army. Discussing her time in the factory, she recalled spending her adolescence "in closed darkness", though she constantly heard air raid sirens and saw American B-29s flying overhead during the day. While attending Nagano Prefectural Matsumoto Arigasaki High School, the wartime deprivation shaped her enduring commitment to personal and creative freedom.
She went on to study nihonga painting at the Kyoto Municipal School of Arts and Crafts in 1948. Frustrated with this distinctly Japanese style, she became interested in the European and American avant-garde, staging several solo exhibitions of her paintings in Matsumoto and Tokyo in the 1950s.


Early success in Japan: 1950–1956
By 1950, she was depicting abstract natural forms in watercolor, gouache, and oil paint, primarily on paper. She began covering surfaces—walls, floors, canvases, and later household objects and nude assistants—with the polka dots that became her signature motif. She held her first solo exhibition in Matsumoto in 1952.
The earliest recorded work in which she incorporated these dots was a drawing in 1939 at age 10, in which the image of a Japanese woman in a kimono, presumed to be the artist's mother, is covered and obliterated by spots. These dotted fields prefigured her large-scale Infinity Nets paintings—some stretching more than 30 feet (9.1 m) in length—which she covered entirely in rhythmic sequences of nets and dots alluding to her hallucinatory visions.
Although never officially affiliated with Surrealism, Kusama engaged with the movement in early gouaches such as A Circus Rider's Dream (1955) and corresponded with poet-critic Shūzō Takiguchi, a leading proponent of Surrealism in Japan.
Regarding her 1954 painting Flower (D.S.P.S.), Kusama recalled:

 One day I was looking at the red flower patterns of the tablecloth on a table, and when I looked up I saw the same pattern covering the ceiling, the windows, and the walls, and finally all over the room, my body and the universe. I felt as if I had begun to self-obliterate, to revolve in the infinity of endless time and the absoluteness of space, and be reduced to nothingness. As I realised it was actually happening and not just in my imagination, I was frightened. I knew I had to run away lest I should be deprived of my life by the spell of the red flowers. I ran desperately up the stairs. The steps below me began to fall apart and I fell down the stairs spraining my ankle.


New York City: 1957–1972
After exhibiting in Matsumoto and Tokyo, Kusama left Japan for the United States in 1957 at the age of 28, finding Japanese society "too small, too servile, too feudalistic, and too scornful of women". Before leaving Japan, she destroyed many of her early works. She remained in Seattle for a year, holding an exhibition of paintings at the Zoe Dusanne Gallery, before relocating to New York City, having corresponded with Georgia O'Keeffe to seek advice on entering the city's art world. Arriving in New York City in 1958, she developed her signature Infinity Nets paintings and early soft sculptures. She achieved critical acclaim with her 1959 solo exhibition at the Brata Gallery and subsequently pioneered body-art performances and happenings. In the United States, she quickly established a reputation as a leading figure in the avant-garde and drew praise from anarchist art critic Herbert Read.
In 1961, she moved her studio into the same building as Donald Judd and sculptor Eva Hesse; Hesse became a close friend. In the early 1960s, Kusama began creating 'Accumulation' soft sculptures by covering everyday objects—such as ladders, shoes, and chairs—with sewn white phallic protrusions. Despite the painstaking intricacy of her works on paper and sculptures, she produced them rapidly and in large quantities, establishing a prolific work ethic that she maintained throughout her life. She also cultivated her public persona, routinely having herself photographed alongside new pieces and appearing in public in signature bob wigs and avant-garde attire.
In June 1963, one of Kusama's soft sculpture pieces, a couch covered with phallus-like protrusions she had sewn, was exhibited at the Green Gallery. The same exhibition included a papier-mâché piece by Claes Oldenburg, who had not previously worked in soft sculpture. Kusama's couch drew significant critical attention, and by September Oldenburg was exhibiting his own sewn soft sculptures, several of which closely resembled Kusama's; Oldenburg's wife, Patty Mucha, apologized to Kusama at the opening. According to Fordham University art historian Midori Yamamura, Kusama's work likely inspired Oldenburg to adopt sewn forms, a medium that propelled him to international stardom and left Kusama deeply depressed. A similar incident followed her Aggregation: One Thousand Boats Show (1963), in which she displayed a rowboat covered in sewn phallic forms inside a room papered floor-to-ceiling with 999 photographic posters of the vessel. Andy Warhol visited the installation and later wallpapered an exhibition space with silkscreened cow imagery to wide acclaim. Growing increasingly guarded about her studio practice, Kusama felt marginalized by the male-dominated New York art world; curator Helaine Posner of the Neuberger Museum of Art later attributed Kusama's lack of equivalent recognition and financial backing to a combination of sexism and racism.

In 1965, Kusama debuted her first infinity mirror installation, Infinity Mirror Room – Phalli's Field, followed by Kusama's Peep Show (also known as Endless Love Show) in 1966. In these purpose-built mirrored chambers, repeated reflections of sculptural forms or colored lights created the illusion of boundless space.
During the following years, Kusama was enormously productive, and by 1966, she was experimenting with room-size, freestanding installations that incorporated mirrors, lights, and piped-in music. She counted Judd and Joseph Cornell among her friends and supporters. However, she did not profit financially from her work. Around this time, Kusama was hospitalized regularly from overwork, and O'Keeffe persuaded her own dealer, Edith Halpert, to purchase several works to help Kusama avoid financial ruin. Unable to earn a sustainable living despite her critical profile, Kusama grew deeply frustrated and attempted suicide.
In 1966, Kusama participated in the Venice Biennale for its 33rd edition. Her Narcissus Garden comprised 1,500 mass-produced, reflective plastic spheres installed outdoors, in what she called a "kinetic carpet". As soon as the piece was installed on a lawn outside the Italian pavilion, Kusama, dressed in a golden kimono, began selling each individual sphere for 1,200 lira (US$2), until the Biennale organizers put an end to her enterprise. Narcissus Garden was as much about the promotion of the artist through the media as it was an opportunity to offer a critique of the mechanization and commodification of the art market.
In the 1960s, Kusama organized outlandish happenings in conspicuous spots like Central Park and the Brooklyn Bridge, often involving nudity and designed to protest the Vietnam War. In one, she wrote an open letter to Richard Nixon offering to have sex with him if he would stop the war. Between 1967 and 1969, she concentrated on performances held with the maximum publicity, usually involving her painting polka dots on her nude performers, as in the Grand Orgy to Awaken the Dead at the MoMA (1969), in which performers were instructed to embrace each other while engaging the sculptures around them at the sculpture garden of the Museum of Modern Art. During the unannounced event, eight performers under Kusama's direction removed their clothing, stepped nude into a fountain, and assumed poses mimicking the nearby sculptures by Picasso, Giacometti, and Maillol.

grok_lead: Yayoi Kusama (22 March 1929 â 14 August 2026) was a Japanese avant-garde artist, painter, sculptor, and author whose oeuvre is defined by obsessive repetition of motifs such as polka dots, nets, and pumpkins, manifesting in paintings, installations, and environmental works that evoke infinity and obliteration. Born in Matsumoto, Nagano Prefecture, into a family operating a seed nursery, Kusama commenced artistic production around age ten, employing polka dots and nets to depict hallucinatory visions of proliferating patterns that engulfed her surroundings. She trained in traditional Nihonga painting before relocating to New York City in 1958, immersing herself in the avant-garde milieu and producing accumulative sculptures and infinity net canvases that intersected with emerging pop art and minimalism. Returning to Japan in the 1970s amid mental health challenges, she resided voluntarily in a Tokyo psychiatric hospital from 1977 until her death, sustaining a voluminous output including mirrored immersion rooms and collaborations with commercial entities like Louis Vuitton. Kusama's recognition escalated in the 21st century with global retrospectives and awards such as the Praemium Imperiale, though her legacy includes scrutiny over passages in her writings portraying Black individuals negatively, prompting a public expression of regret in 2023. Kusama died on 14 August 2026 at a hospital in Tokyo of multiple organ failure.
